title: Naming collisions and an introduction to namespaces
recap: Identifiers that cannot be distinguished in the same scope cause naming collisions. Separate scope regions allow identical simple names to represent different entities.
Standard-library names live in the std namespace. Explicit qualification with the scope-resolution operator identifies the intended name and avoids importing a large collection of possible conflicts.
objectives: Recognize collisions in one file and across linked files.
Explain how scope regions separate identifiers.
Use a qualified standard-library name with the scope-resolution operator.
Avoid broad using-directives at global scope.
warnings: Two indistinguishable global definitions can fail during compilation or linking.
A global using namespace std directive can make otherwise harmless names ambiguous.
Executable statements cannot appear directly at namespace scope.
Mutable global variables increase coupling and should not be introduced casually.
challenge: Create a global function named cout that returns 27. Use the standard output stream with explicit qualification to print the returned number without a naming conflict.
hints: First, change the output expression so its stream is selected explicitly from the std namespace; leave the global cout function unchanged.

Pseudocode: DEFINE global FUNCTION cout: RETURN 27. MAIN: select the cout output stream from the standard namespace; OUTPUT the open-sections label, the result of calling the global cout function, and a newline; return success.
Near-C++ structure: int cout() { return /* required section count */; } int main() { std::cout << /* label */ << cout() << /* newline */; /* return success */ }
